lesson.title: Keys and Values Together: dict.items()
lesson.summary: The items() method returns a live view of key value pairs as tuples, giving you both halves of each entry at once.
lesson.body:
keys() gives you the labels, values() gives you the contents, but plenty of real tasks need both at the same time: printing a receipt line that shows an item name next to its price, or finding which student earned which grade. The items() method is built for exactly this. Calling dictionary.items() returns a dict_items view where each element is a two-value tuple: (key, value).

menu = {"burger": 8.99, "fries": 3.49, "soda": 1.99}
for item in menu.items():
    print(item)

This prints three lines: ('burger', 8.99), then ('fries', 3.49), then ('soda', 1.99), in that order, because dictionaries preserve insertion order. Each line is a single tuple bundling the key and its value together, exactly as items() promises.

print(list(menu.items()))

This prints [('burger', 8.99), ('fries', 3.49), ('soda', 1.99)], the same three tuples collected into an ordinary list, which is a useful way to confirm what items() actually contains before you loop over it.

Like keys() and values(), items() returns a live view, not a frozen copy, and it also updates automatically if the dictionary changes afterward. On its own, printing raw tuples is not usually the end goal. The real power of items() shows up when you unpack each tuple into two separate variables inside a for loop, which is the subject of the next chapter on dictionary iteration.
